summary: Paul opens his final chapter by commending Phoebe, deacon of the church in Cenchreae and his patron, entrusting her with the delivery of the letter. He then greets twenty-six named individuals and several house church communities in Rome, providing an extraordinary window into the diverse, multiethnic leadership of the early church—including Prisca and Aquila who risked their lives for him, and Junia who is prominent among the apostles. Paul warns the church against divisive teachers who create obstacles contrary to sound doctrine, passes on greetings from his Corinthian coworkers including Tertius (the scribe) and Erastus (the city treasurer), and concludes with an apostolic blessing.
whyItMatters: Romans 16 disproves the notion that Paul was an isolated thinker. The chapter reveals the social architecture of early Christianity: women in prominent leadership, diverse socioeconomic backgrounds, and house churches collaborating across the Roman empire.

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Tertius transcribing as amanuensis (16:22).
context.audience: Christian assemblies in Rome, encompassing returning Jewish believers and Gentile converts.
context.date: Circa AD 56–58, near the close of Paul's third missionary journey.
context.setting: Wintering in Corinth or Cenchreae, preparing to deliver the Jerusalem collection before journeying toward Spain.
context.literaryForm: Apostolic letter and theological treatise employing diatribe dialogue, scriptural catena, and pastoral exhortation.

outline.heading: Commendation of Phoebe the Deacon
outline.note: Paul commends Phoebe of Cenchreae as deacon and benefactor, instructing the Roman church to receive her warmly and assist her in her mission.

outline.heading: Greetings to the Roman Urban Network
outline.note: Paul greets twenty-six coworkers and house churches, highlighting Prisca and Aquila, Junia and Andronicus, and diverse laborers in the Lord.

outline.heading: Warning Against Divisive Teachers
outline.note: The assembly is warned to avoid those who cause divisions contrary to doctrine, assured that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet.

outline.heading: Greetings from Corinth and Scribe's Mark
outline.note: Coworkers in Corinth send greetings, including Timothy, Lucius, Jason, Sosipater, Gaius, Erastus the treasurer, and Tertius the letter scribe.

outline.heading: Apostolic Grace Benediction
outline.note: The concluding benediction invoking the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ upon the whole assembly.

keyVerses.text: I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae, that you receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self.
keyVerses.why: Phoebe is commended as diakonos (minister/deacon) and prostatis (benefactor/helper), the courier and likely the first public reader and explainer of Romans.

keyVerses.text: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me.
keyVerses.why: A crucial text acknowledging Junia, a prominent female apostle imprisoned for the faith and senior in Christ to Paul himself.

keyVerses.text: And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
keyVerses.why: Echoes Genesis 3:15, assuring the church that God will defeat the adversary through their unified steadfastness in peace.

questions.question: What was Phoebe's role in delivering and interpreting the letter to the Romans in verses 1–2?
questions.answer: As the designated letter-carrier (commendatus), Phoebe journeyed from Corinth's port of Cenchreae to Rome. In ancient practice, the courier would deliver the letter, read it aloud to the gathering, and answer the recipients' initial clarifying questions.

questions.question: What is the historical significance of calling Phoebe a diakonos and prostatis in verses 1–2?
questions.answer: Diakonos is the same title Paul uses for himself and Timothy (minister/deacon), denoting official congregational ministry rather than informal help. Prostatis means patron or benefactor, indicating she was a woman of independent financial means and social standing.

questions.question: How does the description of Junia in verse 7 impact our understanding of early apostolic ministry?
questions.answer: Paul calls Junia and Andronicus 'notable among the apostles' (episēmoi en tois apostolois). Patristic commentators (such as John Chrysostom) universally recognized Junia as a prominent woman apostle who preceded Paul in the faith.

questions.question: What do the names in verses 3–16 reveal about the social makeup of the Roman house churches?
questions.answer: The twenty-six named individuals include Jewish, Greek, and Latin names; women (ten of the named individuals) and men; enslaved persons or freedmen (Hermas, Ampliatus); and wealthy homeowners (Prisca and Aquila), showing a diverse community.

questions.question: Who are the divisive people Paul warns against in verses 17–19?
questions.answer: Paul warns against teachers who create divisions (dichostasias) and stumbling blocks contrary to the doctrine of mutual love and grace, exploiting naive believers through smooth rhetoric for their own appetites.

questions.question: Who was Erastus 'the treasurer of the city' in verse 23?
questions.answer: Erastus (oikonomos tēs poleōs) held high civic office in Corinth. In 1929, archaeologists in Corinth discovered a 1st-century limestone pavement inscribed: 'Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid this pavement at his own expense,' providing archaeological corroboration.

questions.question: Why did Tertius insert his own greeting in verse 22?
questions.answer: Tertius was the professional scribe (amanuensis) who transcribed Paul's dictation. His personal greeting ('I, Tertius, who write the letter, greet you in the Lord') reveals the collaborative nature of early Christian epistolary composition.

glossary.def: The Greek diakonos, denoting an authorized congregational minister or deacon entrusted with sacred responsibility.
Colleagues (synaichmalōtoi) who shared confinement for the sake of the Christian proclamation.
